title: Poland
hook: Polish rulers invite Jews east, and a great center grows

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Black Death, and two goats in Leviticus. Your line was no scapegoats. Today the road turns east, toward a door that opened.

In a story Jews told about how they came to Poland, refugees tired of being driven from town to town in the west walk east into a forest. They don't know where they are or whether they'll be allowed to stay. And on the trees, or on a slip of paper falling from the sky, depending on who tells it, they find two Hebrew words: po lin. Here, rest. Here, spend the night. So they stayed, and they called the land Polin.
screen: `REFUGEES IN AN EASTERN FOREST.` → `TWO HEBREW WORDS: PO LIN.` → `HERE, REST.`

segments.voice: The legend is wordplay. Polin is the Hebrew name for Poland, and it sounds like po lin, here lodge. It's a folk story, not a historian's account of the name. But it holds something real: for Jews leaving the violence we've followed this week, Poland looked like a place to rest. Behind the legend there are documents. A Polish duke, Bolesław the Pious, issued a charter for the Jews of his lands, known as the Statute of Kalisz, and later Polish kings confirmed and widened it. It protected Jewish lives and property, let Jews trade, and allowed them to run their own courts and synagogues. It even dealt with the lie from Norwich: Jews were not to be accused of using Christian blood, and anyone who made such a charge without proof would be punished. Why invite them? The rulers wanted towns, trade and people who could run markets and keep accounts. The welcome was practical, and never perfect; there would be riots and hard years in Poland too. But over time communities grew, schools grew, and Poland became a home where Jewish learning flourished. When the prophet Jeremiah wrote to exiles in Babylon, he told them to build houses, plant gardens, and "seek the peace of the city" where they had been sent, because their peace was bound up with its peace. In Poland, for centuries, many Jews built houses, planted, and stayed.
screen: `PO LIN: HERE, REST.` · `THE STATUTE OF KALISZ.` · `A PRACTICAL WELCOME.` · then, large: `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Think of someone new in your life: a coworker, a neighbor, a classmate, someone new at your synagogue, church or gym. Picture them a little unsure, still learning where things are, and picture one small way to say, here, you can rest: a name remembered, a question asked, an invitation.
Poland. Polin in Hebrew, read by legend as here, rest. A land whose rulers invited Jews in with a charter of protection, and where a great center of Jewish life grew. Today's word.
Your line: poland invites. A practical welcome, and for centuries, a home. Day nine hundred forty-one, done.
